title: California Fires Rescue Efforts
description: Package about U.S. Army and Air National Guard members working together to stop the fires in Butte Country, Calif. Produced by Staff Sgt. Andrew Hughan.

transcript.text: We are thrilled to have the soldiers, the military come in here.
We don't have enough people. We are spread so thin,
especially with all this lightning that came through,
that we need the soldiers and we need the California National Guard.
We need them to come in here and help us basically build this line.
Building the lines by land and air, encouraging words from CAL FIRE,
the lead agency fighting the devastating wildfires that have been
ripping through the Golden State since the June 21 lightning storm,
ignited dry timber in Butte County, 100 miles north of Sacramento.
Currently 11 states have provided 28 military aircraft and, along with CAL FIRE
and contract assets, dropped nearly 2 million gallons of water
and fire retardant on the flames.
The spirit of cooperation among the flight crews goes a long way
toward successful missions in a rapidly changing fire environment.
At the Chico-Helitac base, a crew from the Utah Army National Guard
is flying a California aircraft, and Nebraska brought a Black Hawk 2.
That's been excellent all the way around. It's no issues, no negative issues.
Everybody's working together as a team to accomplish the mission.
The Army Guard has been flying on fires for several years,
but a California Air National Guard unit has recently been certified
for the bucket missions.
The birds got approved. We had a modified and record time.
The Army was tremendous in giving us assistance and technical knowledge
and getting these aircraft done for us up at May there,
and just very pleased with how everybody just pitched in.
It's basically same team, same fight, and everybody's doing what they have to do
to get the job done.
The 129th Rescue Wing from Moffat Field near San Francisco
is the only Air Force rescue unit certified to drop water on the fires.
Cal Fire has tactical command over the fire,
and when the call came for every available asset, the Guard stepped up to the challenge.
And in the spirit of cooperation from the Guard side of the house,
both in California and Utah, it was fantastic.
We needed the aircraft, and the Guard folks made it happen
so that we could have the Utah crew on the California aircraft
here to support the incident.
By all accounts, experts on the scene forecast a long, hot fire season,
and the expertise learned every day of flying will only help bring this disaster
to a successful conclusion.
In Butte County, California, I'm Air Force Staff Sergeant Andrew Hewitt.
